paragraphs: “What do you think the doctor will say to him?” Kolya asked quickly. “What a repulsive face he has, though, don’t you think? I can’t stand medicine!”
“Ilusha is dying. I think that’s certain,” Alyosha answered sadly.
“They’re crooks! Medicine’s a fraud! I’m glad to have met you, though, Karamazov. I’ve wanted to know you for a long time. I’m only sorry we’re meeting in such sad circumstances.”
Kolya very much wanted to say something warmer and more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed this, smiled, and shook his hand.

“I learned long ago to respect you as a rare person,” Kolya muttered again, faltering and unsure. “I’ve heard you’re a mystic and that you were in the monastery. I know you’re a mystic, but ... that hasn’t put me off. Contact with real life will cure you.... It’s always like that with people like you.”
“What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?” Alyosha was rather astonished.
“Oh, God and all the rest of it.”
“What, you don’t believe in God?”

“Oh, I’ve nothing against God. Of course, God is only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He’s needed ... to keep the universe in order and all that ... and if there were no God, we’d have to invent Him,” added Kolya, beginning to blush. It suddenly struck him that Alyosha might think he was parading his knowledge and trying to prove he was “grown up.” “I don’t have the slightest wish to show off to him,” Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt horribly annoyed.

“Honestly, I can’t stand getting into these discussions,” he said, as if closing the subject. “A person can love mankind without believing in God, don’t you think? Voltaire didn’t believe in God, and he loved mankind, didn’t he?” (“I’m at it again,” he thought to himself.)

“Voltaire believed in God, though not much, I think. And I don’t think he loved mankind much either,” said Alyosha, quietly, gently and quite naturally, as if he were talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck that Alyosha seemed so unsure of his own opinion of Voltaire. It was as though he were leaving the question for him, little Kolya, to decide.
“Have you read Voltaire?” Alyosha finished.
“No, not exactly read.... I read _Candide_, though, in Russian ... in a ridiculous, grotesque old translation ... (At it again! Again!)”
“And did you understand it?”

“Oh, yes, everything.... That is ... Why would you think I couldn’t understand it? There’s a lot of nastiness in it, of course.... Of course I can see it’s a philosophical novel, written to argue for an idea....” Kolya was getting muddled by now. “I’m a Socialist, Karamazov, I’m an incurable Socialist,” he announced suddenly, out of nowhere.
“A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when did you find time to become one? Why, I thought you were only thirteen.”
Kolya winced.

“First of all, I’m not thirteen but fourteen, fourteen in two weeks,” he said, flushing angrily, “and second, I can’t see what my age has to do with it. What matters is what I believe, not how old I am, isn’t it?”

“When you’re older, you’ll see for yourself how age affects what a person believes. I also thought these weren’t your own ideas,” Alyosha answered calmly and modestly, but Kolya interrupted him hotly:

“Oh, come on, you want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit that the Christian religion, for instance, has only ever served the rich and powerful, to keep the lower classes in slavery. That’s so, isn’t it?”
“Ah, I know where you read that, and I’m sure someone told you so!” cried Alyosha.

“Now, what makes you think I read it? And certainly no one told me. I can think for myself.... I’m not against Christ, if you like. He was a most humane person. If He were alive today, He’d be found in the ranks of the revolutionists, and might well play a prominent part.... There’s no doubt about that.”
“Where did you get that, where? What kind of fool have you been making friends with?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Come on, the truth will out! It happens I’ve often talked to Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said that too, so they say.”
“Byelinsky? I don’t remember that. He never wrote it anywhere.”
“Well, if he didn’t write it, they say he said it. I heard it from a ... but never mind.”
“And have you read Byelinsky?”
“Well, no ... not all of him, but ... I did read the passage about Tatyana, about why she didn’t run off with Onyegin.”
“Why she didn’t run off with Onyegin? Surely you can’t ... understand that already?”

“Why, you seem to take me for little Smurov,” said Kolya, with a grin of irritation. “But please don’t think I’m such a revolutionist. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Just because I mention Tatyana doesn’t mean I’m for the emancipation of women. I accept that women are a subject race and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said.” Kolya smiled, for some reason. “And on that question, at least, I’m completely of one mind with that pseudo-great man. I also think that leaving your own country and running off to America is contemptible, worse than contemptible—it’s silly. Why go to America when you can do great service to humanity here? Especially now. There’s a whole mass of fruitful activity open to us. That’s what I answered.”
“What do you mean? Answered whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?”

“I’ll admit they’ve been at me to go, but I refused. That’s between us, of course, Karamazov; do you hear, not a word to anyone. I’m telling this only to you. I’m not at all keen to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember? It’s splendid. Why are you laughing? You don’t think I’m lying, do you?” (“What if he finds out that all I have is that one issue of _The Bell_ from father’s bookcase, and I haven’t read any more of it?” Kolya thought with a shudder.)

“Oh, no, I’m not laughing, and don’t imagine for a moment that you’re lying. No, really, I can’t imagine it, because all this, alas, is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin—_Onyegin_, for instance?... You mentioned Tatyana just now.”
“No, I haven’t read it yet, but I want to. I have no prejudices, Karamazov; I want to hear both sides. Why do you ask?”
“Oh, no reason.”

“Tell me, Karamazov, do you have a terrible contempt for me?” Kolya rapped out suddenly, and drew himself up in front of Alyosha as if he were on parade. “Tell me, please, and don’t beat about the bush.”
“Contempt for you?” Alyosha looked at him in wonder. “Why would I? I’m only sad that a nature as charming as yours should be warped by all this crude nonsense before you’ve even started out in life.”
“Don’t worry about my nature,” Kolya broke in, not without self-satisfaction. “But it’s true that I’m stupidly sensitive, crudely sensitive. You smiled just now, and I thought you seemed to—”

“Oh, my smile meant something quite different. Here’s why I smiled. Not long ago I read what a German who had lived in Russia said about our students and schoolboys today. ‘Show a Russian schoolboy,’ he writes, ‘a map of the stars, which he knows nothing about, and he’ll hand it back to you the next day with corrections on it.’ No knowledge and unlimited conceit—that’s what the German meant to say about the Russian schoolboy.”

“Yes, he’s perfectly right,” Kolya laughed suddenly, “exactly so! Bravo for the German! But he missed the good side, don’t you think? Conceit, maybe, but that comes with youth, and it’ll be corrected if need be. On the other hand, there’s an independent spirit almost from childhood, a boldness of thought and conviction, and none of the spirit of those sausage makers, groveling before authority.... But the German was right all the same. Bravo for the German! Still, Germans need strangling. They may be good at science and learning, but they must be strangled.”
“Strangled, what for?” smiled Alyosha.

“Well, maybe I’m talking nonsense, I agree. I’m awfully childish sometimes, and when I’m pleased about something I can’t hold myself back and I’ll say any rubbish. But look, we’re chattering away here about nothing, and that doctor has been in there a long time. But maybe he’s examining the mamma and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. As I was leaving she suddenly whispered to me, ‘Why didn’t you come before?’ And in such a voice, so reproachfully! I think she’s awfully nice and pitiful.”

“Yes, yes! Well, you’ll be coming often, and you’ll see what she’s like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like that. You’d learn to value a great deal that you’ll find out by knowing them,” Alyosha said warmly. “That would have more effect on you than anything.”
“Oh, how I regret it, and blame myself for not coming sooner!” Kolya exclaimed, in bitter distress.
“Yes, it’s a great pity. You saw yourself how happy the poor child was to see you. And how he fretted, waiting for you to come!”

“Don’t tell me! You’re making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me away was my conceit, my selfish vanity, and that beastly stubbornness I can never get rid of, though I’ve fought it all my life. I see that now. I’m a beast in lots of ways, Karamazov!”
“No, you have a charming nature, though it’s been twisted, and I quite understand why you’ve had such an influence on this generous, painfully sensitive boy,” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And you say that to me!” cried Kolya. “And would you believe it, I thought—I’ve thought several times since I got here—that you despised me! If only you knew how much I value your opinion!”
“But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it, just now, while you were telling your story, I was watching you and thinking that you must be very sensitive!”

“You thought so? What an eye you’ve got, I must say! I bet it was when I was talking about the goose. That was just when I was imagining you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I quite hated you for it, and started talking like a fool. Then I imagined—just now, here—when I said that if there were no God we’d have to invent Him, that I was too eager to display my knowledge, especially since I’d got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn’t showing off out of vanity, though I really don’t know why I did it. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I think it was because I was so pleased ... though it’s perfectly disgraceful to gush the moment you’re pleased, I know that. But I’m convinced now that you don’t despise me; it was all my imagination. Oh, Karamazov, I’m profoundly unhappy. Sometimes I imagine all sorts of things, that everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things.”
“And you torment everyone around you,” smiled Alyosha.
“Yes, I torment everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me, am I very ridiculous now?”

“Don’t think about that, don’t think of it at all!” cried Alyosha. “And what does ridiculous mean? Doesn’t everyone constantly end up being, or seeming, ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people now are terribly afraid of being ridiculous, and that makes them unhappy. What surprises me is only that you feel it so early. I’ve been noticing it for some time, though, and not only in you. Nowadays even children have begun to suffer from it. It’s almost a kind of madness. The devil has taken the form of that vanity and gone into a whole generation; it’s simply the devil,” added Alyosha, without a trace of the smile that Kolya, staring at him, expected to see. “You’re like everyone else,” Alyosha concluded, “that is, like very many others. Only you mustn’t be like everybody else, that’s all.”
“Even if everyone is like that?”

“Yes, even if everyone is. You be the only one who isn’t. You really aren’t like everyone else: just now you weren’t ashamed to own up to something bad, even ridiculous. And who admits that much these days? No one. People have even lost the urge to look critically at themselves. Don’t be like everyone else, even if you’re the only one.”

“Splendid! I wasn’t wrong about you. You know how to comfort a person. Oh, how I’ve longed to know you, Karamazov! I’ve been eager for this meeting for ages. Can you really have thought about me, too? You said just now that you thought of me, too?”
“Yes, I’d heard about you and I had thought of you, too ... and if you’re asking partly out of vanity, that doesn’t matter.”
“Do you know, Karamazov, our talk has been like a declaration of love,” said Kolya, in a bashful, melting voice. “That’s not ridiculous, is it?”
“Not ridiculous at all. And if it were, it wouldn’t matter, since it’s been a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.
“But you know, Karamazov, you have to admit you’re a little ashamed yourself now.... I can see it in your eyes.” Kolya smiled with a sort of sly happiness.
“Why ashamed?”
“Well, why are you blushing?”
“You’re the one who made me blush,” laughed Alyosha, and he really did blush. “Oh, well, I am a little, goodness knows why, I don’t know...” he muttered, almost embarrassed.
“Oh, how I love you and admire you at this moment, just because you’re a little ashamed! Because you’re just like me,” cried Kolya, in sheer ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes shone.
“You know, Kolya, you’re going to be very unhappy in your life,” Alyosha said suddenly, as if something made him say it.
“I know, I know. How you know it all beforehand!” Kolya agreed at once.
“But you will bless life on the whole, all the same.”

“Exactly, hurrah! You’re a prophet. Oh, we’ll get on together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me quite as an equal. But we’re not equals, no, we’re not, you’re better! But we’ll get on. You know, this whole last month I’ve been telling myself, ‘Either we’ll be friends at once, forever, or we’ll part enemies to the grave!’”
“And saying that, of course, you loved me,” Alyosha laughed gaily.
“I did. I loved you terribly. I’ve been loving you and dreaming about you. And how do you know it all beforehand? Ah, here’s the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!”
